question:
Patient note:
A 59-year-old man was brought to the acute care clinic this morning by his partner because, over the preceding forty-eight hours, he noticed that the lower half of his right leg had become visibly larger and increasingly sore whenever he stood up to walk to the bathroom. He recounts that five days ago he developed a febrile influenza-like illness that left him exhausted; aside from getting up to drink water or use the toilet, he remained propped on pillows in bed from Sunday evening through Thursday morning—roughly four and a half consecutive days—streaming television and sleeping for long stretches. By the time the fever and myalgias subsided yesterday, he felt well enough to shower but realized his jogging pants clung tightly around the upper portion of the right calf while hanging loosely on the left. He denies stumbling, weight-lifting, long-distance driving, air travel, insect bites, joint sprain, or localized infection of either lower limb and reports no back pain, groin pull, foot swelling, plantar fasciitis, or recent episodes of cellulitis. He has not felt short of breath, experienced chest discomfort, coughed up blood, had palpitations, or fainted. Review of systems is otherwise unremarkable for fever recurrence, chills, night sweats, unintended weight change, abdominal pain, flank pain, dysuria, or neurologic deficits. His medical history includes well-controlled hyperlipidemia managed with atorvastatin 20 mg nightly and seasonal allergic rhinitis treated with loratadine as needed; he has never been hospitalized for vascular disease, never required anticoagulation, and no first-degree relative has been diagnosed with a clotting disorder before age sixty. He underwent arthroscopic meniscal debridement of the left knee nine years ago without complications and has had no casts, walking boots, or braces since. He does not smoke, drinks two beers on weekend evenings, and denies illicit drug use or testosterone supplementation. Current medications are limited to atorvastatin and loratadine; he has never taken estrogen, selective estrogen-receptor modulators, glucocorticoids, or erythropoiesis-stimulating agents. On arrival—and prior to administration of any analgesic, antipyretic, or anticoagulant—he was seated upright with the right ankle elevated on a pillow. Initial vital signs recorded temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg, heart rate 84 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % while breathing ambient air. Cardiac examination revealed normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs; breath sounds were vesicular throughout, and no wheezes or crackles were appreciated. The abdomen was soft and nontender with no organomegaly. Inspection of the lower extremities showed well-preserved contour of both thighs and ankles, but the mid-posterior compartment of the right calf was fuller than its counterpart. A flexible tape placed 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity measured 42.6 cm on the symptomatic side versus 38.8 cm on the left, establishing a 3.8 cm difference; circumferential assessment 15 cm above the patella revealed symmetric measurements of 55 cm bilaterally, and ankle girth at the malleoli was 24 cm on each side. The skin over the enlarged calf appeared normally pigmented and slightly glossy yet maintained temperature comparable to the contralateral limb. Firm thumb pressure held for five seconds along the anterior tibial crest produced immediate recoil without persistent indentation, and identical pressure on the left leg gave the same result. Gentle but systematic palpation along the course of the femoral canal, popliteal fossa, posterior tibial track, and peroneal corridor elicited a distinct, localized tenderness deep in the medial aspect of the gastrocnemius and along the upper popliteal groove, whereas palpation of adjacent muscle bellies and tendons produced only mild soreness likely related to recent inactivity; no discrete palpable cords, masses, or fluctuant collections were detected. Passive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee extended reproduced a dull ache in the posterior calf but no sharp tearing sensation. Hip, knee, and ankle joints moved through full active range without crepitus or effusion, and straight-leg raise did not provoke back or radicular pain. Distal pulses—posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis—were 2+ and symmetric, capillary refill at all toes was under two seconds, sensation to light touch remained intact, and motor strength in ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion graded 5/5 bilaterally. There were no inguinal or popliteal lymph nodes enlarged on careful palpation. A point-of-care complete blood count and basic metabolic panel drawn before any therapeutic measures revealed hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, platelet count 258 × 10⁹/L, leukocyte count 6.5 × 10⁹/L, serum creatinine 0.96 mg/dL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, aspartate aminotransferase 19 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 17 U/L; international normalized ratio measured 1.0 and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 seconds. Twelve-lead electrocardiography demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 82 beats/min without ST-T segment abnormalities. Plain radiographs of the tibia and fibula obtained by the referring urgent care clinic earlier this morning showed intact cortical margins and only soft-tissue prominence. Because the swelling is confined to the calf, exceeds a three-centimeter circumferential disparity, lacks pitting, arose after several uninterrupted days of bed rest, and is accompanied by reproducible tenderness along the deeper venous trajectory without any musculoskeletal trauma or inflammatory process that would more plausibly account for these findings—despite a deliberate review that excluded muscle strain, ruptured popliteal cyst, cellulitis, lymphedema, chronic venous insufficiency, and popliteal artery aneurysm as leading explanations—duplex sonography of the right lower extremity has been ordered emergently while the patient remains hemodynamically stable in the observation area.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Wells DVT score assigns 1 point per positive risk factor or examination criterion and subtracts 2 if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT. At presentation:
- Bedridden for ≥3 days or recent major surgery: +1 for about 4.5 days of bed rest.
- Localized tenderness along the deep venous system: +1 for focal popliteal and deep calf tenderness.
- Calf swelling ≥3 cm compared with the other leg, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity: +1 because 42.6 − 38.8 = 3.8 cm.
- Entire leg swollen: 0; swelling is confined to the calf.
- Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg: 0; pressure leaves no indentation.
- Active cancer, paralysis/paresis or recent lower-limb cast, collateral nonvaricose superficial veins, and prior DVT: 0 each; none documented.
- Alternative diagnosis at least as likely: 0; no equally likely explanation is identified.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.
Final answer: 3
